169.title: Pauri 4, sound: saachaa saahib
169.hook: saachaa saahib saach naae bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar
169.howItsDone: The fourth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its line on the amrit vela is the scriptural root of the Sikh practice of rising before dawn for simran.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the carefree Giver of pauri three. Your line was the giver never tires. Did you give one thing without keeping count? Day one hundred sixty-nine.

Back in camp three, we set an alarm five minutes early for the amrit vela, the nectar hour before dawn. That hour came from somewhere specific: this pauri, the fourth step of Japji. Today, before we get to the early hours, we hear how the pauri begins. And it begins with a sound you already know. Sach, from aad sach, the true, turns up three times in its very first line, in three different forms, like one word trying on three coats.
screen: `THE ALARM FIVE MINUTES EARLY.` → `IT CAME FROM THIS PAURI.` → `ONE WORD IN THREE COATS.`

segments.voice: The opening line: saachaa saahib, saach naae, bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Let's sound it. Saachaa: SAA-chaa, the true one. Saahib: SAA-hib, Master, Lord; the same sahib you hear in Japji Sahib and Guru Granth Sahib, a word of honor. Saach: the true again, this time about a name. Naae: NAA-ay, name. Bhaakhiaa: BHAA-khi-aa, spoken, expressed. Bhaau: rhymes with how, with a breath on the b; it means love. Apaar: a-PAAR, without limit, boundless. So you can hear the outline already: true Master, true name, spoken with boundless love. Now listen to the sound. Saachaa, saahib, saach: the line opens with three s-sounds in a row, soft and steady, like someone walking up to a door. Then it opens out with bhaakhiaa bhaau, two bh sounds side by side, and ends on the wide, open vowel of apaar. From a narrow door into a very big room. The rest of the pauri carries on in questions: what can we offer, what words can we say? And then a line you've heard before: amrit vela sach naau vadiaaee veechaar, the early hours, the true name, reflecting on its greatness. Then another word we'll open tomorrow: nadar. For now, this pauri is a good one to say slowly, because its first line is almost a whole prayer in miniature: who the One is, what the Name is, and how it's spoken, with love and no limit.
screen: `SAACHAA SAAHIB — TRUE MASTER.` · `SAACH NAAE — TRUE NAME.` · `BHAAU APAAR — BOUNDLESS LOVE.` · `THE AMRIT VELA LINE.` · then, large: `PAURI FOUR.`

segments.voice: Say the first line with me, slowly, out loud if you can. Saachaa saahib, saach naae. Bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Again, a little slower, letting the s-sounds be soft and the last word open wide. Saachaa saahib, saach naae. Bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Once more, almost whispered. Then sit, and notice how your breath lengthened on apaar. Let it stay long. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.

segments.voice: Pauri four. The fourth step of Japji, opening with saachaa saahib: true Master, true name, spoken with boundless love.
Your line: saachaa saahib. Tonight, set that alarm five minutes early again, and say the line once as you do. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

170.title: Pauri 4, meaning: the early hours
170.hook: what can we offer to see His court? In the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name; grace opens the door (Japji 4)
170.howItsDone: Following Japji's fourth pauri, many Sikhs rise in the amrit vela before dawn for simran and Nitnem; nadar, the gracious glance, is spoken of throughout Sikh teaching as what finally opens the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri four. Your line was saachaa saahib: true Master, true name, boundless love. Did the alarm go off a few minutes early this morning? Day one hundred seventy.

What do you bring when you visit someone important? Flowers for a hostess. A bottle of something for the boss. A card and a cake for a new neighbor. We all know the feeling of standing at a door with something in our hands, hoping it's enough. Guru Nanak's fourth pauri stands at a much bigger door, the court of the true Master, and asks exactly that question: what could we possibly bring?
screen: `FLOWERS FOR THE HOSTESS.` → `STANDING AT THE DOOR.` → `WHAT COULD WE BRING?`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. True is the Master, true His name, spoken with boundless love. People ask and beg, give, give, and the Giver gives. Then the questions. What can we place before Him, so that His court comes into view? What words can we speak, so that hearing them He would love us? And the answer, the one camp three built a practice on: in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. Not flowers. Not a bottle. Attention, in the quiet before dawn. Then comes a line people have argued over lovingly for centuries: karmee aavai kaparaa, nadree mokh duaar. Kaparaa is cloth, a garment. Many read it as the body, the robe of this life, which comes by our karma, our actions. Others read karam in its Persian sense, kindness or grace, so that even the robe of honor comes by grace. Either way, the second half is the same: nadree mokh duaar. By His nadar, the door of liberation. Nadar is a glance, a gaze, the look someone gives you when they're glad you came. It's the Persian nazar. In Sikh teaching it's the gracious glance of the One, and the pauri says that's what finally opens the door. So the order is lovely. You show up early. You bring attention, not payment. And the door is opened from the other side. The pauri ends: Nanak, know this; the One is all, and true. You can't buy the glance. You can be awake when it comes.
screen: `WHAT CAN WE BRING TO THE COURT?` · `ATTENTION, BEFORE DAWN.` · `KARAM — ACTION, OR GRACE?` · `NADAR — THE GRACIOUS GLANCE.` · then, large: `THE DOOR OPENS FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The pauri points to the hours before dawn. If it's early where you are, this is that hour. If not, make a small promise now: tomorrow, before the phone, two minutes. For this sit, bring nothing. No requests, no list, no clever words. Just your attention, set down like an empty cup. Breathe. If you pray, you can hold the true Name, Waheguru, and wait. If you don't, simply sit at the door and be awake. The bell holds the time.
Nadar. The gracious glance. In Japji's fourth pauri, by nadar comes the door of liberation.
Your line: the early hour opens. Tomorrow, give the first two minutes of the day to quiet, before anything else asks for you. Day one hundred seventy.

171.title: Pauri 5, sound: thaapiaa na jaae
171.hook: thaapiaa na jaae keetaa na hoe
171.howItsDone: The fifth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its refrain, guraa ik dehi bujhaaee, about the one understanding the Guru gives, is among the best-known lines of the hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar, the gracious glance that opens the door. Your line was the early hour opens. Did the first two minutes of today go to quiet? Day one hundred seventy-one.

Four pauris down. Today we start a new stretch of Japji, pauris five to eight, and it opens with a line built from two short no's. Think of the things people make and set up: a statue in a square, a photo on a shelf, a trophy in a cabinet. We make them, we put them in place, and there they stay. The fifth pauri begins by saying, twice, that the One can't be handled that way. And it says it in a line with a soft, rolling sound.
screen: `A NEW STRETCH: PAURIS 5 TO 8.` → `A STATUE SET IN PLACE.` → `TWO SHORT NO'S.`

segments.voice: The opening line: thaapiaa na jaae, keetaa na hoe. Let's sound it. Thaapiaa: THAA-pi-aa. The th here isn't the English th in thin; it's a t with a puff of breath after it, like the t in top said firmly. Thaap means to set up, to install, to establish, the way an image is set on a pedestal. Na jaae: na, not; JAA-ay, can be. Keetaa: KEE-taa, made. Na hoe: na, not; HO-ay, is, becomes. So you can already hear it: cannot be installed, cannot be made. Two no's, balanced on either side of the line like the two pans of a scale. Then the next line: aape aap niranjan soe. AA-pay aap: himself, by himself. Ni-RUN-jun: stainless, unstained. So: He is Himself, by Himself, the stainless one. Listen to the rhythm of the whole opening: short phrases, each ending on a soft vowel, jaae, hoe, soe. It rocks gently, back and forth. Later in this pauri comes a refrain you'll hear again in the next one, guraa ik dehi bujhaaee. Guraa: Guru. Ik: one. Dehi bujhaaee: give understanding. It's read two ways: as a request, O Guru, give me this one understanding, or as thanks, the Guru has given this one understanding. We'll open what that one understanding is tomorrow. Today just notice that the pauri starts with two no's about what the One is not, and ends with a yes, one understanding, given by the Guru.
screen: `THAAP — TO SET UP, TO INSTALL.` · `TWO NO'S, LIKE A SCALE.` · `AAPE AAP NIRANJAN SOE.` · `GURAA IK DEHI BUJHAAEE.` · then, large: `PAURI FIVE.`

segments.voice: Say the first line with me, slowly, out loud if you can. Thaapiaa na jaae. Keetaa na hoe. Again, and let the breath puff lightly on the th. Thaapiaa na jaae. Keetaa na hoe. Now add the next line. Aape aap niranjan soe. Say all of it once more, softly, and feel it rock back and forth. Then sit, and let the quiet come. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.

172.title: Pauri 5, meaning: one Giver
172.hook: He cannot be installed or made; the Guru has given one understanding, that there is one Giver of all, never to be forgotten (Japji 5)
172.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the fifth pauri each morning; its refrain, that there is one Giver of all beings who should never be forgotten, is often sung as kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri five: thaapiaa na jaae, keetaa na hoe. Your line was thaapiaa na jaae. Did you pass something set in its place and say it? Day one hundred seventy-two.

Have you ever forgotten who gave you something? A sweater you've worn for years, and one day you realize you have no idea where it came from. A habit you picked up from a teacher whose name is gone. We forget givers all the time, not out of ingratitude, just because the gift becomes part of us. The fifth pauri ends with Nanak asking for one thing only: not to forget the Giver.
screen: `A SWEATER, BUT FROM WHOM?` → `THE GIFT BECOMES PART OF US.` → `DON'T FORGET THE GIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. He cannot be installed or made; He is Himself, by Himself, the stainless one. Those who serve Him receive honor. Nanak, sing of the treasure of virtues. Sing, and listen, and keep love in your heart: pain will leave, and peace will come home. Then a run of lines about the Guru's word. Through the Guru comes the sound, through the Guru the scripture, and through the Guru the One is everywhere. The Guru, it says, is Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma; the Guru is Parvati, the mother. Sikhs read this as saying that everything people honor in those great names is found in the Guru's word; Macauliffe and later readers explain it in that sense. Then Nanak says something disarmingly honest: even if I knew Him, I couldn't describe Him; there's no telling it. And then the refrain. Guraa ik dehi bujhaaee: O Guru, give me this one understanding. Sabhnaa jeeaa kaa ik daataa, so mai visar na jaaee: of all living beings there is one Giver; may I not forget Him. Visar is to forget, to let slip from the mind. Na jaaee: may it not happen. That's the whole request. Not wealth, not answers to every question, not even the ability to describe God. Just memory. Because if there is one Giver of everything, then forgetting the Giver is the main thing that can go wrong. And remembering is simran, the practice from camp three, the thing Japji's title word, jap, asks for. It all links up.
screen: `NOT INSTALLED, NOT MADE.` · `SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE.` · `ONE GIVER OF ALL BEINGS.` · `VISAR — TO LET SLIP.` · then, large: `MAY I NOT FORGET.`

segments.voice: Look around you, or picture your room. Pick three things: something you're wearing, something you ate today, something you can hear. For each one, trace it back. Who made it, grew it, carried it, paid for it? Go as far back as you can, until the chain runs out into rain and soil and sun. Notice how many hands there are, and where they all begin. If you pray, you can thank the one Giver, with a single word, Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Pauri five. The One cannot be installed or made; of all beings there is one Giver, and Nanak asks never to forget Him.
Your line: may I not forget. Today, when you use something you were given, a mug, a jacket, a skill, remember who gave it, and where it began. Day one hundred seventy-two.

173.title: Pauri 6, sound: teerath naavaa
173.howItsDone: The sixth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; like the fifth, it ends with the refrain asking the Guru for one understanding, that there is one Giver of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one Giver of pauri five. Your line was may I not forget. Did you remember who gave you something you used today? Day one hundred seventy-three.

Think of a river people travel to. The Ganges at Haridwar, crowded at dawn with people stepping down the ghats into cold water. Or any river, any lake, where someone has gone to wash off a hard year. Guru Nanak knew those places well; the stories say he walked to many of them. The sixth pauri of Japji opens on the riverbank, with a line about bathing. And it's one of the most musical lines in the hymn: two words that rhyme, side by side, like two feet stepping into water.
screen: `STEPS DOWN INTO A RIVER.` → `WASHING OFF A HARD YEAR.` → `TWO WORDS THAT RHYME.`

segments.voice: The opening line: teerath naavaa, je tis bhaavaa. Let's sound it. Teerath: TEE-rath. A teerath is a pilgrimage place, a holy ford, a spot on a river where people bathe. Naavaa: NAA-vaa, I would bathe. Je: jay, if. Tis: tiss, to Him. Bhaavaa: BHAA-vaa, I were pleasing. So you can hear it: I would bathe at the holy place, if I were pleasing to Him. And listen to the rhyme: naavaa, bhaavaa. The two halves of the line land on the same sound, like an echo. Then the line goes on: vin bhaane ke naae karee. Vin: without. Bhaane: pleasing. Ke: what. Naae karee: bathing would I do. Without pleasing Him, what bathing would I do? We'll open that tomorrow. Today, notice the music. Guru Nanak builds this pauri from rhyme and repetition, easy to carry in your head. And it has more of those sounds as it goes. There's a line with a string of treasures in it: ratan, javaahar, maanik, jewels, gems and rubies; you can hear their weight just in the sound. And then, again, the refrain you met in pauri five: guraa ik dehi bujhaaee. O Guru, give me this one understanding. When a refrain repeats, it's telling you what to hold onto. Two pauris in a row end on the same request. By now you might know it by heart. Say it in the practice if you do.
screen: `TEERATH — A HOLY FORD.` · `NAAVAA, BHAAVAA — A RHYME.` · `RATAN, JAVAAHAR, MAANIK.` · `THE REFRAIN COMES BACK.` · then, large: `PAURI SIX.`

segments.voice: Say the first line with me, slowly, out loud if you can. Teerath naavaa. Je tis bhaavaa. Again, and let the rhyme ring: naavaa, bhaavaa. Teerath naavaa. Je tis bhaavaa. Once more, softly. Then, if you can, add the refrain from pauri five: guraa ik dehi bujhaaee. Then sit. Picture cool water around your feet, and just breathe. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Pauri six. The sixth step of Japji, opening with teerath naavaa: I would bathe at the holy place, if I were pleasing to Him.
Your line: teerath naavaa. Next time you wash your face or your hands today, say the line once, slowly, while the water runs. Day one hundred seventy-three.

174.title: Pauri 6, meaning: jewels within
174.hook: pilgrimage bathing is worth it only if it pleases Him; the mind holds jewels when it hears the Guru's teaching (Japji 6)
174.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the sixth pauri each morning; its line about jewels in the mind is often quoted to explain why Sikhs give so much weight to listening to Gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri six. Your line was teerath naavaa. Did you say it once with the water running? Day one hundred seventy-four.

There's an old story people tell in many cultures: a man spends his whole life traveling the world looking for treasure, and comes home poor, and then finds it buried under his own kitchen floor. It's a story people keep retelling because it keeps being true. We go looking far away for what's close. Guru Nanak's sixth pauri says something like it, standing on the riverbank we met yesterday. The jewels, it says, are closer than the river.
screen: `TREASURE UNDER THE KITCHEN FLOOR.` → `LOOKING FAR FOR WHAT'S CLOSE.` → `CLOSER THAN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. If I please Him, that is my pilgrimage bath; if I don't, what good is bathing? I look at the whole creation: without His grace, what does anyone receive? And then: mat vich ratan javaahar maanik, je ik gur kee sikh sunee. In the mind there are jewels, gems and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. Mat is the mind, the understanding. Ratan, javaahar, maanik: three words for precious stones, piled up so you feel the weight. And the key is sikh, which here means a teaching, an instruction. It's the same root as the word Sikh itself: a learner, one who receives the teaching. So a Sikh is someone who listens for the jewels. Notice what the pauri doesn't say. It doesn't mock anyone for bathing in a river. Guru Nanak stood at those rivers, the stories say, and people still come to them. It says the bath is only as good as the heart that steps into it, and that what really washes and enriches a person is inside, waiting to be heard. Then the refrain returns: O Guru, give me this one understanding, that there is one Giver of all beings; may I not forget Him. The jewels were never imported from somewhere else. They're what's left when one teaching is actually heard. One. Not a library. A single line, taken in, can do it.
screen: `A BATH IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE HEART.` · `MAT — THE MIND.` · `RATAN, JAVAAHAR, MAANIK.` · `SIKH — ONE WHO HEARS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `JEWELS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Look inward, as if you're opening a small box you haven't opened in a while. Look for one jewel in yourself. Not something you've achieved. Something you are. Patience that shows up when it matters. A way of making people laugh. The kind of attention you give a friend in trouble. When you find one, hold it for a moment, and ask where it came from: who taught you, what line you once heard and kept. If you pray, you can thank the Giver with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Pauri six. The bath is worth it only if it pleases Him, and the mind holds jewels, gems and rubies, when it hears even one teaching of the Guru.
Your line: jewels within. Today, tell someone about a jewel you see in them. One sentence, plainly said. Day one hundred seventy-four.

175.title: Pauri 7, sound: je jug chaare
175.hook: je jug chaare aarjaa hor dasoonee hoe
175.howItsDone: The seventh pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its long opening line about living through the four ages is one of the most memorable in the hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jewels of pauri six. Your line was jewels within. Did you tell someone about a jewel you see in them? Day one hundred seventy-five.

If you could live as long as you wanted, how long would you choose? A hundred years? A thousand? People have always dreamed about it, from old legends of sages who lived for ages to today's headlines about slowing down aging. The seventh pauri of Japji opens with that dream, and makes it enormous: a life as long as all four ages of the world, and then ten times more. It's a line about time, and it sounds like it's stretching.
screen: `HOW LONG WOULD YOU CHOOSE?` → `FOUR AGES OF THE WORLD.` → `THEN TEN TIMES MORE.`

segments.voice: The opening line: je jug chaare aarjaa, hor dasoonee hoe. Let's sound it. Je: jay, if. Jug: like the English word jug, but shorter, closer to joog; it's an age, an era. You met it inside jugaad, through the ages. Chaare: CHAA-ray, all four. In Indian thought, time turns through four great ages, the four jugs. Aarjaa: AAR-jaa, a lifespan. Hor: and more. Dasoonee: da-SOO-nee, tenfold. Hoe: HO-ay, it were. So: if your lifespan were all four ages, and ten times more. Tomorrow, the meaning, and a surprising twist. Today, the sound. Listen to how the line opens with short, quick words, je, jug, and then gets longer: chaare, aarjaa, dasoonee. The syllables themselves stretch, like the lifetime they describe. The next lines keep adding: nav khandaa vich jaaneeai, known in all nine regions of the world. Naal chalai sabh koe, with everyone walking along beside you. Changaa naau rakhaae kai, keeping a good name. Jas keerat jag lei, praise and fame in the world. Each line piles something on: long life, fame, followers, reputation. It's the sound of a list getting bigger and bigger. And then, just when the list is at its tallest, the pauri turns with a single short word: je. If. Hold on to that. The turn is tomorrow. For now, enjoy the sound of the dream: je jug chaare aarjaa.
screen: `JUG — AN AGE. CHAARE — ALL FOUR.` · `AARJAA — A LIFESPAN.` · `THE LIST GETS BIGGER.` · `THEN ONE SHORT WORD: IF.` · then, large: `PAURI SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Say the first line with me, slowly, out loud if you can. Je jug chaare aarjaa. Hor dasoonee hoe. Again, and let the long words stretch. Je jug chaare aarjaa. Hor dasoonee hoe. Once more, softly. Then sit, and feel how long this one breath is, this one moment. It's the only length of life you actually have in your hands right now. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ਜੇ ਜੁਗ ਚਾਰੇ ਆਰਜਾ ਹੋਰ ਦਸੂਣੀ ਹੋਇ ॥`

segments.voice: Pauri seven. The seventh step of Japji, opening with je jug chaare: if your life lasted all four ages, and ten times more.
Your line: je jug chaare. And look back at this week: saachaa saahib, nadar and the early hour, thaapiaa na jaae, one Giver, teerath naavaa, and jewels within. Day one hundred seventy-five.

fork.setup: the pauri's list is at its tallest: long life, fame, followers, a good name. what short word turns it?
fork.reveal: je, if. the turn comes tomorrow.

original.script: ਜੇ ਜੁਗ ਚਾਰੇ ਆਰਜਾ ਹੋਰ ਦਸੂਣੀ ਹੋਇ
original.say: jay jug CHAA-ray AAR-jaa, hor da-SOO-nee HO-ay
original.note: Gurmukhi: the opening of Japji's seventh pauri, Ang 2.

trapdoor: what you thought: living forever.
what it means: a life through all four ages and ten times more, the start of a list of everything the world admires.
what a scholar hears: the four jugs are the Indian ages of the world, Sat, Treta, Dvapar and Kal; the pauri borrows the scale to make a point about grace.
